s0003.literal: Lu Zilong; Qian Daoji; Luo Ya
s0003.idiomatic: Lu Zilong; Qian Daoji; Luo Ya

s0004.literal: Lu Zilong, styled Xingshi, was a native of Wu in Wu commandery.
s0004.idiomatic: Lu Zilong, styled Xingshi, came from Wu in Wu commandery.

s0005.literal: His grandfather Changzhi was Liang magistrate of Jiaxing.
s0005.idiomatic: His grandfather Changzhi had been magistrate of Jiaxing under Liang.

s0006.literal: His father Quan was magistrate of Feng.
s0006.idiomatic: His father Quan was magistrate of Feng.

s0007.literal: Zilong in youth was generous and high-minded and aspired to merit and fame.
s0007.idiomatic: As a youth Zilong was open-handed and ambitious, hungry for achievement and renown.

s0008.literal: He began his career as a direct attendant in the Eastern Palace.
s0008.idiomatic: He entered service as a direct attendant in the eastern palace.

s0009.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion he gathered followers in his home district.
s0009.idiomatic: When Hou Jing rebelled he raised men in his home district.

s0010.literal: At that time Zhang Biao was Administrator of Wu commandery and took him on as a commander.
s0010.idiomatic: Zhang Biao was then administrator of Wu and made him a field commander.

s0011.literal: When Biao moved his garrison to Kuaiji, Zilong followed him.
s0011.idiomatic: When Biao shifted his headquarters to Kuaiji, Zilong went with him.

s0012.literal: When Emperor Wen campaigned against Biao, Biao's generals Shen Tai, Wu Baozhen, Shen Jin, and others all surrendered, but Zilong fought hard and was defeated; Emperor Wen honored his loyalty, had him again lead his old command, and commissioned him military adjutant of the central guard.
s0012.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen moved against Biao, Biao's generals Shen Tai, Wu Baozhen, Shen Jin, and the rest surrendered—but Zilong fought on and lost. Emperor Wen admired his constancy, restored him to his old troops, and brevetted him military adjutant of the central guard.

s0013.literal: He served in succession as magistrate of Shifeng and Yongxing counties.
s0013.idiomatic: He served in turn as magistrate of Shifeng and Yongxing.

s0014.literal: When Hua Jiao held Xiang province in rebellion, because Zilong lay in his very heartland Jiao deeply feared him and repeatedly sent envoys to win him over; Zilong would not yield, so Jiao sent troops to attack him but could not overcome him.
s0014.idiomatic: Hua Jiao rebelled and held Xiang province. Zilong sat in his heartland, so Jiao feared him and sent envoys again and again to lure him over. Zilong refused. Jiao then attacked but could not break him.

s0015.literal: When Jiao was defeated at Yingzhou, Zilong led troops to strike his rear and thereby joined the imperial army.
s0015.idiomatic: When Jiao fell at Yingzhou, Zilong marched out to hit his rear and joined the imperial troops.

s0016.literal: He was given the staff, made Regular Attendant of Direct Communication, and Commander of Military Affairs in Wuzhou; his rank was advanced to marquis and his fief increased together with the previous to seven hundred households.
s0016.idiomatic: He received the staff, was made regular attendant of direct communication and commander of military affairs in Wuzhou, was raised to marquis, and his fief was brought to seven hundred households in all.

s0017.literal: Soon he was transferred to Commander of Military Affairs in the three provinces of Jing, Xin, and You, made Manifest Resolution General and Inspector of Jing, the staff and regular attendant unchanged.
s0017.idiomatic: Soon he was made commander of Jing, Xin, and You, manifest-resolution general and inspector of Jing, keeping the staff and his attendant title.

s0018.literal: At that time Jing province had been newly established, with its seat at Gong'an; the walls were not yet secure; Zilong built the ramparts, soothed and gathered Chinese and barbarians alike, won the people's hearts exceedingly, and at the time was acclaimed as fulfilling his charge.
s0018.idiomatic: Jing province was new then, with its seat at Gong'an and its walls still weak. Zilong raised the fortifications, settled Chinese and non-Chinese alike, and won deep goodwill. Men of the day called him equal to the post.

s0019.literal: In the third year, officials and people went to the capital and submitted a memorial asking that a stele be erected to praise his achievements; an edict approved it.
s0019.idiomatic: In the third year the officials and people went to court with a memorial asking for a stele to honor his work. The throne approved.

s0020.literal: In the first year of Taijian he was advanced in title to Cloud-Banner General.
s0020.idiomatic: In the first year of Taijian (569) he was promoted to cloud-banner general.

s0021.literal: In the second year he died, aged forty-seven.
s0021.idiomatic: He died in the second year (570), at forty-seven.

s0022.literal: Posthumously he was made Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant; his posthumous name was Wei.
s0022.idiomatic: He was posthumously made scattered-cavalry regular attendant, with the posthumous name Wei.

s0024.literal: Zhiwu at sixteen led his father's old army; he followed Wu Mingche on the northern campaign with merit, rose to chief clerk of a princely establishment and Administrator of Hongnong, and still served under Mingche.
s0024.idiomatic: At sixteen Zhiwu took over his father's troops. He followed Wu Mingche north, earned merit, rose to a princely chief clerk and administrator of Hongnong, and remained under Mingche.

s0025.literal: When Mingche was defeated at Lüliang, Zhiwu fled home and was killed by others, aged twenty-two.
s0025.idiomatic: When Mingche was broken at Lüliang, Zhiwu fled home and was murdered, aged twenty-two.

s0026.literal: Zilong's younger brother's son Cai also had resource and plan; he followed Zilong on campaigns with merit, was made Administrator of Nanping, enfeoffed as Viscount of Shixing county, Editorial footnote marker 2. fief three hundred households.
s0026.idiomatic: Zilong's nephew Cai had talent and nerve. He campaigned with Zilong, was made administrator of Nanping, and enfeoffed as Viscount of Shixing [2] with three hundred households.

s0027.literal: He followed Wu Mingche on the northern campaign, supervised An province, and garrisoned at Suyu.
s0027.idiomatic: He marched north with Wu Mingche, supervised An province, and held Suyu.

s0028.literal: He was made advisory military adjutant to the Central Guard Prince of Shixing, then transferred to Whirlwind Fierce General and Inspector of Xin.
s0028.idiomatic: He became advisory military adjutant to the central guard prince of Shixing, then whirlwind-fierce general and inspector of Xin.

s0029.literal: In the thirteenth year of Taijian he died, aged forty-two.
s0029.idiomatic: He died in the thirteenth year of Taijian (581), at forty-two.

s0030.literal: Posthumously he was made Supernumerary Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant.
s0030.idiomatic: He was posthumously made supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0031.literal: Qian Daoji, styled Zitao, was a native of Changcheng in Wuxing.
s0031.idiomatic: Qian Daoji, styled Zitao, came from Changcheng in Wuxing.

s0032.literal: His father Jingshen was Liang magistrate of Hanshou.
s0032.idiomatic: His father Jingshen had been magistrate of Hanshou under Liang.

s0033.literal: Daoji in youth was famed for filial conduct; when grown he had considerable resource and plan; in the Founder's early days the Founder gave him a cousin in marriage.
s0033.idiomatic: Daoji was known early for filial piety and, grown, showed real capacity. In the Founder's lean years the Founder married him to a cousin.

s0034.literal: He followed in the pacification of Lu Zilue at Guangzhou and was made magistrate of Binjiang.
s0034.idiomatic: He took part in pacifying Lu Zilue at Guangzhou and was made magistrate of Binjiang.

s0035.literal: When the Founder acted as regent he sent Daoji to follow Emperor Wen in pacifying Zhang Biao at Kuaiji; for merit he was made Direct-Gate General, Supernumerary Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant with credentials, and Inspector of East Xuzhou, enfeoffed as Marquis of Yong'an with a fief of five hundred households.
s0035.idiomatic: While the Founder held regency he sent Daoji with Emperor Wen to crush Zhang Biao at Kuaiji. For merit he was made direct-gate general, supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant with credentials, and inspector of East Xuzhou, and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yong'an with five hundred households.

s0036.literal: He still led three thousand armored troops, followed Hou Andu to garrison and defend Liangshan, and soon also held the magistracies of Qiantang and Yuhang counties.
s0036.idiomatic: He still commanded three thousand armored men, joined Hou Andu in garrisoning Liangshan, and soon held Qiantang and Yuhang as well.

s0037.literal: In the third year of Yongding he followed Emperor Wen in garrisoning at South Wan Ford.
s0037.idiomatic: In the third year of Yongding (559) he followed Emperor Wen to garrison South Wan Ford.

s0038.literal: In the first year of Tianjia he also held the magistracy of Shan, garrisoning at the county's Southern Cliff; soon he was made Administrator of Linhai, his garrison at the cliff unchanged.
s0038.idiomatic: In the first year of Tianjia (560) he added the magistracy of Shan and garrisoned the county's Southern Cliff. Soon he was made administrator of Linhai while keeping that post.

s0039.literal: When Hou Andu campaigned against Liu Yi, Daoji led troops out through Songyang to cut his rear.
s0039.idiomatic: When Hou Andu attacked Liu Yi, Daoji marched through Songyang to sever his retreat.

s0040.literal: When Yi was pacified, for merit he was made Bearer of the Staff, Regular Attendant of Direct Communication, Light-Carriage General, Commander of Military Affairs in the two Heng provinces east and west, and Inspector of Heng, concurrently Interior Administrator of Shixing.
s0040.idiomatic: After Yi was suppressed he received the staff, was made regular attendant of direct communication, light-carriage general, commander of the eastern and western Heng provinces, and inspector of Heng, and still held Shixing as interior administrator.

s0041.literal: In the first year of Guangda his fief was increased together with the previous to seven hundred households.
s0041.idiomatic: In the first year of Guangda (567) his fief was brought to seven hundred households in all.

s0042.literal: In the second year of Taijian he again followed Zhaoda in campaigning against Xiao Kui at Jiangling; Daoji separately commanded the massed armies with Lu Zilong to burn the green-mud fleet, then served as Zhaoda's vanguard, attacked Ancheng, and reduced it.
s0042.idiomatic: In the second year of Taijian (570) he again followed Zhaoda against Xiao Kui at Jiangling. Daoji separately commanded the allied armies with Lu Zilong to burn the green-mud ships, then led Zhaoda's van, took Ancheng, and received its surrender.

s0043.literal: For merit he was advanced to Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant and Benevolent Martial General; his fief was increased together with the previous to nine hundred households.
s0043.idiomatic: For merit he was made scattered-cavalry regular attendant and benevolent-martial general, his fief rising to nine hundred households in all.

s0044.literal: That year he was transferred to Benevolent Prestige General and Administrator of Wuxing.
s0044.idiomatic: That year he was made benevolent-prestige general and administrator of Wuxing.

s0045.literal: Before he took up the post he was reassigned Bearer of the Staff, Commander of Military Affairs in the three provinces of Ying, Ba, and Wu, and Inspector of Ying.
s0045.idiomatic: Before he went out he was reassigned with the staff as commander of Ying, Ba, and Wu and inspector of Ying.

s0046.literal: When the imperial army marched north to campaign, Daoji with the yitong officer Huang Faqu besieged Liyang.
s0046.idiomatic: When the imperial troops marched north, Daoji and the yitong officer Huang Faqu besieged Liyang.

s0047.literal: When Liyang city was pacified, Daoji was left to garrison it.
s0047.idiomatic: When Liyang fell he was left to hold the city.

s0048.literal: For merit he was advanced to Cloud-Banner General; his fief was increased together with the previous to one thousand five hundred households.
s0048.idiomatic: For merit he was promoted to cloud-banner general, his fief brought to one thousand five hundred households in all.

s0049.literal: That year, in the eleventh month, he fell ill and died, aged sixty-three.
s0049.idiomatic: That year, in the eleventh month, he sickened and died, aged sixty-three.

s0050.literal: Posthumously he was given his former office; his posthumous name was Su.
s0050.idiomatic: He was posthumously granted his last office, with the posthumous name Su.

s0052.literal: Luo Ya, styled Qimen, Editorial footnote marker 3. was a native of Lin'an in Wuxing.
s0052.idiomatic: Luo Ya, styled Qimen, [3] came from Lin'an in Wuxing.

s0053.literal: His grandfather Midao was Liang field-cadet in the Prince of Ancheng's establishment.
s0053.idiomatic: His grandfather Midao had been field-cadet in the Prince of Ancheng's staff under Liang.

s0054.literal: His father Yu was military adjutant of the central guard to the Prince of Poyang, heir to the kingship.
s0054.idiomatic: His father Yu was central-guard military adjutant to the Prince of Poyang, heir to the kingship.

s0055.literal: At twelve, a kinsman skilled in physiognomy said, "This boy's countenance is extraordinary; he will surely reach far."
s0055.idiomatic: At twelve a clansman skilled in faces said, "This lad's looks are not ordinary. He will go far."

s0056.literal: At the end of Liang's Taiping era Emperor Wen once took refuge at Lin'an; Ya's mother Ling, Editorial footnote marker 4. saw Emperor Wen's bearing, knew he was no ordinary man, and entertained him with great courtesy.
s0056.idiomatic: At the end of Liang's Taiping era Emperor Wen once sheltered at Lin'an. Ya's mother Ling [4] saw his bearing, knew he was no common man, and received him with deep courtesy.

s0057.literal: When Emperor Wen became Administrator of Wuxing he took Ya on as a commander; Ya followed him in pacifying Du Kan, Zhang Biao, and others; in every battle he always took the van and broke the line, Editorial footnote marker 5. his courage topped all the armies; for merit he was made Direct-Gate General.
s0057.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen became administrator of Wuxing he made Ya a commander. Ya followed him against Du Kan, Zhang Biao, and the rest, always first through the breach; [5] his bravery outshone every unit. For merit he was made direct-gate general.

s0058.literal: In the second year of Taiping he left office for his mother's mourning.
s0058.idiomatic: In the second year of Taiping (557) he left office to mourn his mother.

s0059.literal: When Emperor Wen garrisoned Kuaiji he was recalled to serve as magistrate of Shanyin.
s0059.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen held Kuaiji he was recalled as magistrate of Shanyin.

s0060.literal: In the third year of Yongding he was made military adjutant of the central guard in the Pacifying East establishment and went out to garrison Yecheng.
s0060.idiomatic: In the third year of Yongding (559) he was made central-guard military adjutant in the pacifying-east staff and went out to hold Yecheng.

s0061.literal: Soon he followed Emperor Wen in resisting Wang Lin at South Wan.
s0061.idiomatic: Soon he followed Emperor Wen against Wang Lin at South Wan.

s0062.literal: When Emperor Wen took the throne he was given credentials, made Might-Subduing General and Supernumerary Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, enfeoffed as Marquis of Chang'an county, Editorial footnote marker 6. fief five hundred households.
s0062.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen succeeded he was given credentials as might-subduing general and supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant, and enfeoffed as Marquis of Chang'an [6] with five hundred households.

s0063.literal: Soon he was made magistrate of Lin'an, then transferred to Inspector of Yue; the rest unchanged.
s0063.idiomatic: Soon he was magistrate of Lin'an, then inspector of Yue, his other titles unchanged.

s0064.literal: Earlier, when Ya's mother died, famine and war raged; only now was she buried; an edict posthumously honored Ya's mother as Grand Madam of Chang'an state, posthumous name Gong.
s0064.idiomatic: When his mother had died, famine and war made burial impossible. Only now was she laid to rest. An edict posthumously honored her as Grand Madam of Chang'an state, with the posthumous name Gong.

s0065.literal: Ya was transferred to Faithful Prestige General and Administrator of Jinling.
s0065.idiomatic: Ya was made faithful-prestige general and administrator of Jinling.

s0066.literal: In the third year, for merit in pacifying Zhou Di, he was transferred to Champion General and Interior Administrator of Linchuan.
s0066.idiomatic: In the third year, for pacifying Zhou Di, he was made champion general and interior administrator of Linchuan.

s0067.literal: In the third year of Taijian he was given Pacifying Distance General and Interior Administrator of Hengyang; before he took up the post he was moved to Administrator of Guiyang.
s0067.idiomatic: In the third year of Taijian (572) he was made pacifying-distance general and interior administrator of Hengyang. Before he went out he was shifted to administrator of Guiyang.

s0068.literal: In the eighth year he returned to court and was transferred to Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, entering direct service in the palace offices.
s0068.idiomatic: In the eighth year (577) he returned to court as scattered-cavalry regular attendant on duty in the palace offices.

s0069.literal: In the tenth year he was given Inspector of Feng; the rest unchanged.
s0069.idiomatic: In the tenth year (579) he was made inspector of Feng, his other titles unchanged.

s0070.literal: In the second year of Zhide he died, aged fifty-seven.
s0070.idiomatic: He died in the second year of Zhide (584), at fifty-seven.

s0071.literal: Posthumously he was made Pacifying Distance General and Inspector of Guangzhou.
s0071.idiomatic: He was posthumously made pacifying-distance general and inspector of Guangzhou.

s0073.literal: The historiographer says: Lu Zilong and Qian Daoji—one brought his whole household to follow, the other was an old companion who raised merit from the first—both had talent to command and were fit to bear the army's trust.
s0073.idiomatic: The historiographer writes: Lu Zilong and Qian Daoji—one brought his house to follow, one stood with the Founder from the first—both could lead and were trusted with the armies.

s0074.literal: As to receiving border appointments and achieving merit together—how fine!
s0074.idiomatic: Given frontier command and shared achievement—how fine indeed!

s0075.literal: Luo Ya recognized true worth and served it; he knew Emperor Wen's heaven-granted virtue—was he not next to Zhang Liang?
s0075.idiomatic: Luo Ya saw true worth and served it; he knew Emperor Wen bore heaven's mandate—was he not Zhang Liang's peer?

s0076.literal: Ya's mother, wise and foreseeing, matched the rite of Bo Valley; the gentleman knows that keen judgment reaching far—was it not here?
s0076.idiomatic: Ya's mother, wise before the fact, matched the courtesy of Bo Valley. A gentleman will say that vision reaching far lived here.

s0078.literal: Soon he followed Hou Andu in resisting Wang Lin at
s0078.idiomatic: Soon he followed Hou Andu in resisting Wang Lin at

s0084.literal: Enfeoffed as Viscount of Shixing county—"Shixing" in the History of the Southern Dynasties reads "Shikang."
s0084.idiomatic: On "enfeoffed as Viscount of Shixing county": the History of the Southern Dynasties reads Shikang.

s0085.literal: Luo Ya styled Qimen—"Luo Ya" in the History of the Southern Dynasties reads "Luo Wenya."
s0085.idiomatic: On "Luo Ya styled Qimen": the History of the Southern Dynasties reads Luo Wenya.

s0086.literal: Ya's mother Ling—"Ling" in the Hall edition reads "Chen."
s0086.idiomatic: On "Ya's mother Ling": the Hall edition reads Chen.

s0087.literal: Textual verification says "'Chen' is corrupt as 'Ling' in all editions; now follows the History of the Southern Dynasties."
s0087.idiomatic: Textual verification holds that Chen is corrupt for Ling in all editions; the text now follows the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0088.literal: In every battle always took the van—"always" (zhe) was missing in the original and is supplied from the various editions.
s0088.idiomatic: On "in every battle always took the van": zhe (always) was missing in the base text and is restored from other editions.

s0089.literal: Enfeoffed as Marquis of Chang'an county—by examination "Chang'an" should follow the History of the Southern Dynasties and read "Lin'an."
s0089.idiomatic: On "enfeoffed as Marquis of Chang'an county": examination shows Chang'an should follow the History of the Southern Dynasties as Lin'an.

s0090.literal: Below, "Chang'an state" should likewise follow the History of the Southern Dynasties and read "Lin'an state."
s0090.idiomatic: Below, "Chang'an state" should likewise follow the History of the Southern Dynasties as Lin'an state.
